summary: A best current practice document on how unicast address allocation policies affect Internet routing. It argues that addresses should be handed out in ways that let routes be grouped together, so routing tables stay manageable.

plainLanguage.summary: If street numbers follow the neighborhood layout, a mail carrier needs a short list. Handing out addresses in an orderly way keeps the routing map small.

subtitle: Why handing out IP addresses that follow network topology keeps Internet routing tables from collapsing.

tldr.problem: If every organization owns portable IP addresses wherever it connects, routes cannot be grouped together and the routing system would grow until it broke.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC contrasts "address ownership" with "address lending", where addresses come from a provider's block and are returned when the customer leaves, so providers can advertise one aggregated prefix.
tldr.outcome: It recommends formally adding address lending to the allocation policies and strongly encouraging organizations that do not provide aggregation to use it, accepting that they will need to renumber.

today: RFC 2008 is a Best Current Practice published in October 1996. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 2008 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 7) about unicast IP address allocation and management for the Public Internet. It does not try to settle who should set address policy. It lays out the technical issues that any policy must respect and makes recommendations.

Its focus is two policies: address ownership and address lending. An IESG note says the authors, the reviewing working group and the IESG concluded that no other currently deployable technology can overcome these limitations, and that the constraints could be reviewed if routing or router technology advances enough.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper asks how we should hand out Internet addresses so the Internet keeps working as it grows. It compares two ways of giving out addresses.

sections.title: Address Value and Hierarchical Routing
sections.content:
The RFC argues that an IP address gets its intrinsic value from reachability: its ability to interact with the Public Internet routing service. If the routing system stopped operating, addresses would lose their functional value there, and every allocation policy would be meaningless.

Hierarchical routing is the only proven mechanism for scaling routing to the current size of the Internet. It groups the addresses covered by part of the topology into a single route, and it can do this recursively. The RFC compares it to the phone network, where a switch keeps one entry for a whole area code rather than every subscriber.

For this to work, addresses must reflect the network topology. That can happen in two ways: constrain the topology to match address assignment, or let topology change freely and change an entity's address to match. Changing an address is called renumbering.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone numbers work because a country code and area code tell the phone company which direction to send a call. Internet addresses should work the same way: where an address is on the map tells routers where to send things.

sections.title: Scaling the Routing System
sections.content:
Before CIDR was introduced, the growth rate had doubled the routing table roughly every nine months, while computer capacity doubles roughly every 24 months. The RFC says routers could not keep up, so mechanisms that contain routing information growth are essential. Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) has been deployed since late 1992, and without it the routing system would already have collapsed.

As an example, in October 1995 AlterNet had 3194 routes inside its network but advertised only 799 to the rest of the Internet, a saving of 2395 routes (75%). CIDR aggregation resulted in less than 30,000 routes in the default-free part of the Internet routing system.

Not everything aggregates. Pre-CIDR allocations, unconnected sites with old allocations, and sites that switch provider while keeping their addresses all inject exceptions. Each exception harms scalability, and unbridled growth in exceptions will cause the routing system to collapse.
sections.plainLanguage: Grouping many small routes into one big route saves a lot of space. But every house that keeps its old number and moves to a different street needs its own special entry, and too many of those make the list unmanageably long.

sections.title: Address Ownership Versus Address Lending
sections.content:
Under address ownership, address space once allocated stays with the organization as long as it wants it and is called "portable". The RFC says this was never explicitly stated but was always assumed and practiced by Internet Registries. Because the Internet's topology is not constrained, the RFC concludes that without new mechanisms, you can have ownership for everyone or a routable Internet, but not both. Ownership for everyone would lead to a breakdown and a partitioned Internet.

Under address lending, an organization gets addresses on loan. The loan terms must say the addresses are returned if the borrower is no longer contractually bound to the lender and the lender can no longer provide aggregation. The borrower must then get new addresses and renumber. The RFC expects providers to use lending, coupling the loan to the service agreement, and to arrange enough aggregation. Lending may also be applied hierarchically, so one loan ending can affect organizations that borrowed from it.

The RFC strongly recommends a grace period after disconnection: at least 30 days, and no longer than six months to contain routing overhead. It also warns that even without an explicit lending policy, renumbering may still be needed to keep Internet-wide connectivity when changing providers, because some providers may refuse to accept a longer prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: Owning an address is like owning a phone number you keep forever, no matter where you live. Lending is like getting a number from your local phone company that you give back when you leave. The second way keeps the phone book short.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
Organizations that can provide reachability to a sufficiently large fraction of destinations through a single prefix can reasonably be given ownership-style addresses, because their route will be maintained in the default-free part of the Internet. Within such organizations, the RFC suggests address lending.

For all other organizations that want Internet-wide connectivity, the RFC recommends address lending, which means they eventually need to renumber when they first connect or change their attachment. Carrying routes costs money, and organizations with non-aggregatable addresses should be prepared to absorb that cost themselves. Neither policy alone guarantees Internet-wide connectivity, so sites should ask their providers what reach and cost to expect.

An organization that does not need Internet-wide connectivity may use ownership addresses and reach the rest of the Internet through mediating gateways such as application layer gateways or NATs. That avoids renumbering but has other drawbacks. To lower renumbering costs, the RFC says organizations should be strongly encouraged to deploy tools such as DHCP and to use the DNS. Because IPv6 allocation is based on CIDR, the recommendations apply to IPv6 too.
sections.plainLanguage: Big companies that can speak for lots of the Internet can keep their own numbers. Everyone else should borrow numbers from their provider and be ready to switch if they move.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Renumbering affects security policy at the renumbering site and at sites that regularly communicate with it. Firewalls that decide on source addresses must be reconfigured when the site renumbers, or when an outside site that is granted access renumbers.

The RFC says it is highly inadvisable to rely on unauthenticated source or destination IP addresses for security decisions, because address spoofing is not difficult. It points to the IP Authentication Header (RFC 1826) and the IP Encapsulating Security Payload (RFC 1827) as better approaches. It also says authentication is strongly desirable in any renumbering mechanism, since otherwise an adversary could renumber systems that should not be renumbered.
sections.plainLanguage: Guards who check the return address on a letter can be fooled by fake labels. Moving to a new address means telling the guards, and the process of telling them should be secured.
